title: Relayed — sync
description: Phase 2: the ordered log, delivery, catch-up and the write path. Metrics and events read from Loki because the sink emits them as log records; the trace panels read from Tempo, which is a separate OTLP signal (OBSERVABILITY.md §10b).

panels.title: What happened to THIS message — traces
Slowest sends, compose → ack
panels.description: The client span that opens when somebody presses return and closes when the ack lands. It spans the queue wait, so an offline send is a long span rather than a missing one. Click a row for the whole path, including the server span that assigned the ordinal.

panels.title: Writes the server refused
panels.description: A refusal is one nack on one socket and one red message for one person. `nack_code` says which rule refused it; the parent trace says who was sending and into which chat.

panels.title: Reconnect — hello → welcome
panels.description: The client span that opens when a socket attempt begins and closes when `welcome` lands, with `hello` and `welcome` as marks inside it. Click through for the server half: `sync.hello` carries the actor, the workspace, the negotiated protocol and how big the welcome frame was. A slow reconnect is visible here as one span rather than as an absence.

panels.title: Invariants — for these, absence is health
Telemetry dropped — is this dashboard COMPLETE?
panels.description: Records the OTLP buffer refused because it was full. The one number every other number here depends on: a load run once dropped 86% of its telemetry and said nothing, so every count was a twelfth of the truth while the shapes still looked right. MUST be 0.

panels.title: Slow consumers dropped
panels.description: Connections disconnected mid-fanout for an oversized backlog. A sustained rate means people are silently losing live delivery and falling back to catch-up on every event — which feels like a laggy app and logs nothing.

panels.title: Cursors stalled (invariant 1)
panels.description: Behind, answered, and STILL not moving. Not merely behind — a client back from a week offline is behind and perfectly healthy. This is a hole nothing is going to fill, and it is otherwise completely silent.

panels.title: Malformed frames
panels.description: A frame that parsed as JSON and failed its body schema. Unlike an unknown frame — which is version skew working as designed — this is a bug at one end or the other.

panels.title: Unknown events applied (invariant 32)
panels.description: An op advanced the cursor without being applied: an old client meeting a new op type. Expected to rise after a release and fall as people update (RELEASE.md — updates are opt-in). Sustained means somebody is stuck.

panels.title: Engine failures caught (sync.failed)
panels.description: The error boundary caught something the engine could not do and carried on. MUST be 0. Before it existed a throw in the apply loop reached a socket event handler and killed the process, so the only record was a stack trace on stderr. A caught failure leaves the frontier where it was, so a persistent one becomes sync.cursor.stalled a heartbeat later — read them together.

panels.title: Staged events held out of order
panels.description: Invariant 1's other half. Staged events collapse the moment the revision before them lands, so this should sit at or near zero. A depth that never falls is the same failure as a stalled cursor, seen from the other side.

panels.title: Frames ignored, by reason
panels.description: `unknown` is invariant 43 working — a newer peer naming something this build predates. `malformed` is a bug. `denied` is somebody asking for a stream they cannot read. Counted together so the three stay comparable.

panels.title: How ops left the outbox
panels.description: `acked` is the happy path. `failed` is a red message somebody has to act on. `coalesced` is a send-then-delete that correctly never touched the network (invariant 6) — a success, not a loss.

panels.title: Server write latency, by op
panels.description: Gate, allocate, append, commit. The first question about a slow send is whether the time is ours or the network's, and this is the half a client cannot measure about itself.

panels.title: Outbox depth
panels.description: Ops waiting, sampled at every drain. Depth growing while a socket is live means acks are not coming back — invisible to a user until they notice nothing they typed has a timestamp.

panels.title: Oldest unsent op
panels.description: Depth alone cannot tell these apart: sixty ops from the last minute and one op stuck for an hour are the same depth. Unbounded while offline, which is correct rather than alarming.

panels.title: Writes refused, by op
panels.description: A refusal reaches exactly one person as one nack. Nothing else aggregates them, and somebody who cannot post may simply stop trying.

panels.title: Sends, deletes and everything appended
panels.description: Events committed to the log, by stream kind. Chat traffic and directory churn grow for entirely different reasons, which is why they are split.

panels.title: Connected sockets
panels.description: The denominator for every rate on this dashboard — a fanout count means nothing without it — and the line that drops to zero in an outage while every other counter merely stops emitting, which looks like a quiet night.

panels.title: Fanout audience, by stream
panels.description: How many actors one event resolves an audience of. Delivery is O(audience) per event by design; this is the number that says when that stops being free. A workspace stream reaches everyone, hence the split.

panels.title: Commit → bytes on the wire
panels.description: The half of delivery latency no client can see or report: from the outside it is indistinguishable from a slow network.

panels.title: Applying a batch, client side
panels.description: The write that competes with the reads in `ui.query.duration`. Read as a pair, the two say whether chunking the apply is still buying anything.

panels.title: Catch-up: replayed or gapped
panels.description: A rising gap share means the threshold or the retention horizon is wrong (invariant 25). Every gap costs a client all the history below the tail it is handed.

panels.title: Replay size against the 500 cap
panels.description: What makes GAP_THRESHOLD a measured number rather than one somebody picked. If p99 sits at 500, the cap is what is producing the gaps — not the clients.

panels.title: Catch-up server time, by answer
panels.description: The per-request cost a reconnect storm multiplies. Ten thousand clients returning at once is the load spike this system actually has (invariant 31).

panels.title: Cursor lag (invariant 1)
panels.description: server_head_rev minus synced_through_rev, sampled per sweep. Lag that rises and falls is catch-up working. Lag that rises and stays is the silent failure this whole design is arranged against.

panels.title: Gaps entered, by stream
panels.description: The client-side half of the catch-up counter: gaps a client actually acted on, rather than ones the server offered.

panels.title: Backfill pages pulled
panels.description: Read against `sync.gap` this is what a gap actually COSTS: a gap nobody scrolls back through is free, and one everybody scrolls through is not.

panels.title: Directory syncs
panels.description: A failed directory sync is message authors rendering as monograms. The page count is deliberately not tracked — it is ceil(actors / page size), a number we already hold; whether the pager FINISHED is the question.

panels.title: Sockets closing, by cause
panels.description: Why everybody reconnected, in one query. A deploy, expired tokens, clients being killed and zombie sockets are four different incidents that look identical from a connection count alone.

panels.title: Attempts before a welcome
panels.description: How many tries a reconnect took. Flat at zero is healthy — and was flat at zero for a different reason until step 13, because the event read the counter after resetting it and had never once said anything.

panels.title: Welcome frame size
panels.description: How close `welcome` is to needing to page. Max is the interesting line: the largest workspace hits the ceiling first, and it hits it for everybody in that workspace at once.

panels.title: Chats per actor
panels.description: The number that PREDICTS the ceiling rather than reporting it afterwards. OBSERVABILITY §9 names this one specifically as the example of a signal that gives advance warning of a design limit.

panels.title: Appended against swept
panels.description: The log's net growth. A sweep falling behind appears here long before it appears as disk, and the gap between the lines is what sizes the table.

panels.title: Everything the engine reported
panels.description: Ids live here and are forbidden as metric labels — traces and logs are indexed for high cardinality and metrics are not (§5). This is where "why did THIS person's message hang" becomes answerable.
